transcript.text: dyson keeps pulsin on n off like its stutterin, wont stay on proper. batt is full. pls help

That pulsing on and off is a Dyson's way of protecting itself. It's nearly always telling you the airflow is restricted rather than that something has broken. Since the battery's full, the likely causes in order are: 1. A clogged or slightly damp filter. This is the most common cause by far.
2. A blockage somewhere in the wand, floorhead or bin inlet.
3. Less often, the battery not seating properly, or a worn battery that drops out under load even though it shows full. Work through these checks with it switched off and, if your model allows, the battery taken out: 1. Empty the bin. Then take out the filter (usually at the top or the back of the main body) and wash it in cold water only, with no detergent, until the water runs clear. Leave it to dry for at least 24 hours. If it's even slightly damp it will still pulse. If the filter was grubby or damp, that's very likely your culprit. If it's torn or misshapen, it needs replacing.
2. Take the wand and floorhead off and look through each piece. A coin dropped down the wand should fall straight through. Also check the hole where air enters the bin. If you find fluff, hair or a sock stuck in there, clear it and that should fix it.
3. Turn the floorhead over and pull any hair or thread off the brush bar. Check it spins freely by hand. A jammed roller can also make it cut in and out.
4. Try it with just the main body, no wand or head. If it runs steadily that way, the blockage is in the wand or head. If it still pulses with nothing attached, a clean dry filter and a full battery, suspect the battery contact or the battery itself. If it still pulses once the filter is clean and fully dry and everything is clear, the battery is the next suspect. Let me know what you find and we'll go from there.
its a v8 animal. just did the handheld only test, still pulses but a bit less. emptied the bin too, was rammed with dog hair, still pulsin

That's useful. Because it still pulses with the wand and head off, the problem is in the main body. Pulsing a bit less suggests some of the restriction has gone, but not all of it. A bin rammed with dog hair usually means a lot of fine dust and hair has also been pulled through to the filter. That makes the filter the strongest suspect now. 1. Take the filter out. It's usually a twist-off unit on the main body. Leave it somewhere warm for a full 24 hours. If it was grey and caked, that's probably your problem. Only judge it once it's completely dry, because a damp filter pulses too.
2. With the bin off, look at the fine metal mesh around the cyclone, and up into the inlet where air comes into the bin. Dog hair often wraps tightly round that mesh. Pick it off by hand, or brush it off with a dry brush. Don't put water near the motor end. If it was matted, that could be the rest of the restriction.
3. If it now runs steadily, you're sorted. If it still pulses with a clean, dry filter and a clear mesh and inlet, the battery becomes the main suspect. Batteries on V8-age machines often wear out, and a worn one can show full yet drop out under load. Check the battery is firmly seated and the contacts are clean. If that's fine, a worn battery would be the likely part. Let me know what the filter and mesh look like.
mesh and inlet were a bit dusty, wiped it. filter is grey not purple lol, never touched it in 3 yrs. no burning smell or heat or anything tho. do i just leave it out dry or wash it?

Switch it off and unplug it (or take the battery off) first. Wash it. Drying it alone won't help, because a filter that's grey after three years is packed with fine dust. That dust is very likely what's choking the airflow and making it pulse. 1. Hold the filter under a cold tap. Use no detergent or soap. Run water through it and gently tap it out against the sink. This can take several rinses.
2. Shake out the excess water. Leave it somewhere warm and airy for at least 24 hours, longer if you can. Don't put it on a radiator or in a tumble dryer, and don't use a hairdryer, as heat can warp it.
3. Don't run the vacuum without the filter in. That lets dust straight into the motor.
4. Refit the filter only when it's bone dry, then try the vacuum. It may not go back to bright purple, and that's fine. What matters is that water passes through it freely. If it's torn or misshapen, it needs replacing. The same goes if it still looks clogged after a good wash. It's reassuring that there's no burning smell or heat. That makes a motor problem unlikely. If it runs steadily with the clean, dry filter, you're sorted. Just wash the filter every month or so, especially with a dog. If it still pulses with a clean, dry filter and clear airways, the battery becomes the likely culprit. A three-year-old V8 battery can show full but cut out under load. Check that it's clipped in firmly and the contacts are clean before going further. Let me know how it runs once the filter's dry.
[Helpful to see: image "Poor suction — what to check first" — A vacuum that pulses or cuts out after running is usually a full bin, a dirty filter or a blockage starving the airflow — check and clear those before suspecting battery, charger or motor. Switch off and unplug first. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
ok washed it, water came out black lol. left it overnight on the radiator side. pulses way less but still a bit

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
Pulsing way less is a good sign. It means the filter was the main restriction. The bit that's left is most likely the filter itself still, for two reasons. Overnight usually isn't long enough for a pleated filter to dry right through the middle, even next to a radiator. And water coming out black after three years means one wash often doesn't get all the fine dust out. 1. Take the filter out again and rinse it under the cold tap until the water runs clear, however many rinses that takes. No soap.
2. Leave it somewhere warm and airy for a full 24 to 48 hours. If it feels even slightly cool or heavy, it's still damp.
3. While it's drying, check the bin clicks fully shut and its seal sits flat. A small air leak or a bin that isn't seated can upset it too.
4. Refit the bone-dry filter and try it. If it runs steadily, it was the filter, and a monthly wash will keep it that way with a dog around. If it still pulses with a properly clean, fully dry filter and clear airways, the battery is the likely culprit. A three-year-old V8 battery can show full but sag under load. First take it off, wipe the contacts and refit it firmly. If that doesn't help, a replacement battery is the likely part. I can't confirm the exact battery that fits your V8 Animal, so get it from Dyson's own spares (they can match it to the serial number on the machine) or a reputable repairer. Cheap unbranded batteries are best avoided. With no burning smell or heat, a motor fault looks unlikely, so it shouldn't need an engineer unless a new battery doesn't sort it.
ok will rinse it again. also found a big clump of hair and cat litter stuck down the bottom of the wand where the head goes on, pulled it out. will test once filter is dry

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
Good find. A clump of hair and cat litter at the bottom of the wand would most likely choke it when the wand and head are on, so that's one restriction gone. It doesn't explain everything, though, because it still pulsed a bit with just the main body. That's why the filter is still the main suspect for whatever pulsing is left. While the filter dries, a couple of quick things:
1. Turn the floorhead over and check the brush bar and the neck where it joins the wand for more litter or hair. If litter got into the wand, some has probably ended up in the head too. Make sure the bar spins freely by hand.
2. When the filter is bone dry, test it two ways: first handheld only, then with the wand and head on. If it runs steadily both ways, you're sorted. If it's fine handheld but pulses with the head on, there's still something in the head or wand.
3. If it still pulses handheld only, with a properly dry, clean filter, the battery is the likely part. Before buying one, take the battery off, wipe the contacts and refit it firmly. I couldn't confirm the exact battery match for your V8 Animal. If it comes to that, Dyson's own spares can match it using the serial number on the machine, or a reputable vacuum repairer can. Let me know how the test goes.
tested it after the filter dried, its fine now, proper suction, no pulsin. checked the brush bar too, bit of hair, cut it off

[Heading: Likely cause: battery — flat or failed (cordless)]
It was a restricted-airflow problem all along. The three-year-old filter was doing most of the choking, and the clump of hair and litter in the wand added to it. The pulsing was the V8 protecting its motor, not a fault, so nothing's broken and the battery sounds fine. 1. Wash the filter every month in cold water only, no soap. Let it dry naturally for a full 24 hours. Having a spare filter makes this painless, because you can swap one in while the other dries.
2. Empty the bin before it gets rammed, and give the mesh a quick brush now and then.
3. Snip the hair off the brush bar every few weeks.
4. Try not to hoover up cat litter in bulk if you can help it, as it's heavy and tends to jam the wand neck. If it ever starts pulsing again, check the filter and the wand first, just like this time. Is there anything else I can help with?
